questions.text: Regarding somatosensory area 1 all are correct, Except
questions.explanation: True: It is present in the parietal lobe, behind the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus (postcentral). B False: The sizes of these areas are directly proportional to the number of specialized sensory receptors in each area of the body. C False: Neurons of the somatosensory cortex are arranged in vertical columns extending all the way through the six layers of the cortex. Each column detects a specific sensory modality. The most anterior columns respond to muscle, tendon, and joint stretch receptors. Posteriorly columns respond to slowly adapting cutaneous receptors. More posterior columns are sensitive to deep pressure. The most posterior columns respond only when a stimulus moves across the skin. D False: The body and face are mapped in the contralateral cortex. E False: Somatosensory area 1 gives origin to some of the pyramidal tract fibers (40%).
questions.keyConcept: True: It is present in the parietal lobe, behind the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus (postcentral)
options: Size of representation depends on number of receptors.
Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation.

questions.text: The withdrawal reflex is initiated by stimulation of which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: C. True: cutaneous nerve endings are the receptors responsible for perception of painful stimulus (nociceptors). A., D. False: muscle spindle and golgi tendon are responsible for stretch reflex and inverse stretch reflex. B., E. False: Joint capsule receptors are proprioceptors and Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors.
questions.keyConcept: C

questions.text: Reflex contraction of the extensor muscles of the right leg can occur following
questions.explanation: A True: contraction of extensor muscles of right leg occurs in response to their stretch or in response to withdrawal reflex in the left leg. This withdrawal reflex could be elicited by hitting the left foot (crossed extensor reflex). B False: stretch of flexors in right leg leads to their contraction. C False: stretch of flexors of left-hand lead to their contraction. D False: excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg will lead to reflex relaxation and not contraction. E False: painful kicking of the right knee will lead to flexor muscle contraction of the right leg and extensor muscle contraction of left leg (crossed extensor reflex).
questions.keyConcept: A True: contraction of extensor muscles of right leg occurs in response to their stretch or in response
options: Hitting a chair with the left foot.
Stretching the flexor muscles in the right leg
Stretching of the flexor muscles in left hand
Excessive stretch of extensors of the right leg
Painful kicking of the right knee.

questions.text: The phenomenon of decerebrate rigidity can be explained, at least in part, by which of the following?
questions.explanation: D True: decerebrate rigidity means lesion in lower midbrain (between superior and inferior colliculi) or Damage to upper pons. As, the pontine reticular formation has its intrinsic stimulatory effect on stretch reflex, so it is working unopposed by the lost inhibitory effect of cortical and subcortical structures leading to rigidity. It is marked rigidity with extension of both upper and lower limbs. A False: 1b sensory fibers are afferents from Golgi tendon organs receptors when stimulated lead to relaxation of the muscle. B False: cerebellar input to red nucleus is inhibitory to stretch reflex. C True: medullary reticular formation is inhibitory to stretch reflex. E False: nigrostriatal degeneration as in parkinsonism where rigidity is all over the movement with more affection of flexor muscles.
questions.keyConcept: D True: decerebrate rigidity means lesion in lower midbrain (between superior and inferior colliculi) or Damage to upper
options: Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus.
Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control.
Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei.

questions.text: Concerning headache:
questions.explanation: Headache is an example of referred pain, in which pain from deep structures is felt at the body surface. Migraine can be triggered by emotions and is commonly accompanied by nausea and vomiting.
questions.keyConcept: Headache is an example of referred pain.
options: It is only caused by intracranial causes
It is only caused by extracranial causes
It is an example of referred pain
Nausea and vomiting are not symptoms occurring during a migraine attack

questions.text: Concerning referred pain:
questions.explanation: Referred pain always accompanies visceral pain and is felt in a somatic area sharing the same dorsal root as the affected viscus. It is explained by the convergence projection and convergence facilitation theories.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain always accompanies visceral pain.
options: It is felt in the somatic structure innervated by a different dorsal root from that innervating the diseased viscus
It can't be explained by convergence projection theory
It can't be explained by convergence facilitation theory

questions.text: In a neurological examination, while performing the cotton wool test:
questions.explanation: The cotton wool test assesses crude (light) touch, which is detected by rapidly adapting cutaneous mechanoreceptors. The sensation is carried by large myelinated fibers rather than C fibers only.
questions.keyConcept: Light touch is detected by cutaneous mechanoreceptors.
options: The receptors are moderately adapting receptors
The cotton is felt better on the palmar side of the hands
The sensation tested is carried on C fibers only
The sensation tested is fine touch

questions.text: Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:
questions.explanation: Tissue damage releases kinins such as bradykinin, which are potent activators of nociceptors. They sensitize and stimulate pain endings to produce the sensation of pain.
questions.keyConcept: Kinins released by tissue damage stimulate pain receptors.

questions.text: Pain sensation can be inhibited by:
questions.explanation: Stimulation of opioid receptors activates the descending analgesia system and inhibits pain transmission. Pain receptors do not adapt, and naloxone blocks rather than enhances analgesia.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid receptor stimulation inhibits pain sensation.
options: Stimulation of the lateral spinothalamic tract
Increasing the pain threshold by kinin

questions.text: Slow pain:
questions.explanation: Slow pain is carried by C fibers and its pathway activates the non-specific thalamic nuclei, producing poorly localized, long-lasting pain. Fast pain, by contrast, travels in A-delta fibers to the sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Slow pain activates the non-specific thalamic nuclei.
options: Is perceived mainly in the sensory cortex
Pathway activates the non-specific thalamic nuclei
Is carried along type A delta fibers

questions.text: Specificity:
questions.explanation: Specificity means each receptor responds best to one particular form of energy, its adequate stimulus. The Weber-Fechner law instead describes the relationship between stimulus intensity and sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Each receptor is most sensitive to its adequate stimulus.
options: Is also termed the Weber-Fechner law
Means that each receptor is most sensitive to a specific form of energy called the adequate stimulus
Is a state of partial depolarization
Is due to high intensity of the stimulus

questions.text: The analgesia system includes:
questions.explanation: The descending analgesia system includes the peri-aqueductal gray of the midbrain, which projects to the raphe magnus nucleus in the medulla. These centers inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
questions.keyConcept: The peri-aqueductal gray is part of the analgesia system.
options: The peri-aqueductal area in the mid-brain
Raphe magnus nucleus in the posterior horn of the spinal cord

questions.text: The fast pain sensation that accompanies a painful trauma is carried to the C.N.S. by fibres that belong to:
questions.explanation: Fast, sharp, well-localized pain is conducted by small myelinated A-delta fibers. Slow pain is instead carried by unmyelinated C fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is carried by A-delta fibers.

questions.text: Tic douloureux:
questions.explanation: According to the answer key, tic douloureux is treated here as an example of secondary hyperalgesia. It is typically a unilateral, sharp lancinating pain.
questions.keyConcept: Tic douloureux is presented as an example of secondary hyperalgesia.
options: Is an example of secondary hyperalgesia
Is due to convergence facilitation theory
Is due to sensitization of pain receptors by chemicals
Sharp lancinating pain in the distribution of the facial nerve

questions.text: Regarding somatosensory area 1, all are correct EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Somatosensory area 1 lies in the postcentral gyrus, which is posterior, not anterior, to the central sulcus. Its columnar organization, contralateral representation and contribution to the pyramidal tract are all correct.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to the central sulcus.
options: Has columns that are specialized to receive one type of sensation
Lies anterior to the central gyrus
Size of representation depends on number of receptors

questions.text: Tactile discrimination is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Tactile (two-point) discrimination depends on rapidly adapting cutaneous mechanoreceptors and is perceived in the sensory cortex. Muscle spindles are proprioceptors, not tactile receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Tactile discrimination is a rapidly adapting cutaneous sensation.
options: It is tested through a two marker test
Perceived at the level of the thalamus

questions.text: The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory Area 1:
questions.explanation: Crude touch is perceived at the thalamic level rather than requiring somatosensory area 1. Fine discriminative modalities such as vibration, proprioception and stereognosis depend on the cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch is perceived at the thalamus, not somatosensory area 1.

questions.text: Migraine headache typically begins with prodromal symptoms such as nausea, loss of vision, visual aura or other sensory hallucination. Which one of the following is thought to be the cause of such prodromes?
questions.explanation: The migraine prodrome is attributed to vasospasm causing ischemia and disrupted neuronal activity in the relevant sensory cortex. The subsequent vasodilation phase produces the throbbing headache.
questions.keyConcept: Migraine prodromes are caused by vasospasm and cortical ischemia.
options: Vasospasm leading to ischemia and disruption of neuronal activity in the relevant sensory area of the cortex
A selective loss of GABA neurons in the various sensory areas of cortex
Increased blood flow to brain tissue in the visual or other sensory cortex

questions.text: Fill in the blanks: The adequate stimulus for the muscle spindle is change in muscle ___, while the adequate stimulus for the Golgi tendon organ is change in muscle ___.
questions.explanation: The muscle spindle lies in parallel with the muscle fibres, so it is excited by changes in muscle length (stretch). The Golgi tendon organ lies in series within the tendon, so it senses changes in muscle tension generated during contraction. Together they provide complementary feedback for length and force control.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles detect length changes while Golgi tendon organs detect tension changes.

questions.text: Compare between nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibres.
questions.explanation: Both fibre types are the intrafusal fibres of the muscle spindle but signal different aspects of stretch. Nuclear bag fibres, with their central clump of nuclei and Ia endings, respond to the velocity of stretching (dynamic response). Nuclear chain fibres, with nuclei in a row and type II endings, encode the steady length of the muscle (static response).
questions.keyConcept: Nuclear bag fibres (Ia) sense dynamic stretch; nuclear chain fibres (II) sense static length.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear bag fibres: thick and short, with nuclei clustered in a central bag; innervated by primary (Ia, annulospiral) endings; mainly detect the dynamic (rate) component of stretch. Nuclear chain fibres: thin and long, with nuclei arranged in a single row; innervated chiefly by secondary (type II, flower-spray) endings; mainly detect the static (sustained length) component of stretch.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks: The arrangement of the muscle spindle within skeletal muscle is ___, while the arrangement of the Golgi tendon organ is ___.
questions.explanation: Because the muscle spindle is arranged in parallel with the extrafusal muscle fibres, it is stretched when the muscle lengthens and unloaded when the muscle contracts. The Golgi tendon organ is arranged in series within the tendon, so it is activated by the tension produced during contraction. This geometric difference explains why one monitors length and the other monitors force.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with muscle fibres; Golgi tendon organs lie in series.

questions.text: Enumerate the components of the central analgesia system and their neurotransmitters. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: The central (descending) analgesia system suppresses pain transmission from the brain down to the spinal cord. Activation of the periventricular area and periaqueductal gray, using endorphins and enkephalin, excites the raphe magnus nucleus, which sends serotonergic fibres to the dorsal horn. There the pain inhibitory complex releases enkephalin to block incoming C and A-delta fibre signals both pre- and postsynaptically.
questions.keyConcept: Descending analgesia uses the PVA, PAG, raphe magnus and dorsal-horn enkephalin to block pain.
questions.modelAnswer: Periventricular area (PVA): secretes beta-endorphins. Periaqueductal gray (PAG): secretes enkephalin. Raphe magnus nucleus (RMN): secretes serotonin. Pain inhibitory complex (PIC) in the dorsal horn: secretes enkephalin, producing pre- and postsynaptic inhibition of incoming C and A-delta pain fibres.

questions.text: Compare fast and slow pain. (3 Marks)
questions.explanation: Pain is conducted by two fibre populations with different properties. Fast (first) pain travels in thinly myelinated A-delta fibres, giving a sharp, well-localised sensation that warns of injury immediately. Slow (second) pain travels in unmyelinated C fibres, producing a dull, aching, poorly localised and persistent sensation that follows the initial pain.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain (A-delta) is sharp and immediate; slow pain (C fibres) is dull and delayed.
questions.modelAnswer: Fast pain: carried by A-delta fibres; sharp, well localised, and felt immediately. Slow pain: carried by C fibres; dull, aching, poorly localised, and delayed in onset.

questions.text: Compare the intrafusal fibres: nuclear chain versus nuclear bag fibres. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: The muscle spindle contains two kinds of intrafusal fibres that signal different aspects of stretch. Nuclear bag fibres, with their central clump of nuclei and Ia primary endings, respond mainly to the rate (dynamic phase) of stretch. Nuclear chain fibres, with nuclei in a row and type II secondary endings, signal the static sustained length of the muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Nuclear bag fibres (Ia) sense dynamic stretch while nuclear chain fibres (II) sense static length.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear chain fibres: thin and long, with nuclei arranged in a single row; innervated mainly by type II (secondary) sensory endings; signal the static (sustained) length of the muscle. Nuclear bag fibres: thick and short, with nuclei clustered together in a central bag; innervated by type Ia (primary) sensory endings; signal the dynamic (rate) of stretch.

questions.text: Define headache and enumerate its intracranial and extracranial causes. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: Headache is a form of referred pain in which deep pain-sensitive structures such as vessels, meninges and sinuses project the sensation onto the scalp surface. Intracranial causes act by stretching, inflaming or altering pressure on pain-sensitive structures (e.g., meningitis, tumour, low CSF pressure, hypertension). Extracranial causes arise from nearby structures such as the eyes, paranasal sinuses, muscles or teeth.
questions.keyConcept: Headache is referred pain from deep head structures with intracranial and extracranial causes.
questions.modelAnswer: Headache: referred pain felt on the surface of the head, arising from deep pain-sensitive structures. Intracranial causes: meningitis, brain tumour, decreased CSF pressure, fever, and hypertension. Extracranial causes: glaucoma, sinusitis, emotional stress, and dental (tooth) disorders.

questions.text: Explain the mechanisms of referred pain. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: Referred pain occurs because visceral and somatic inputs share central pathways. In the convergence-projection mechanism, both inputs synapse on one dorsal horn neuron, and the brain, more used to somatic signals, localises the pain to the skin. In the convergence-facilitation mechanism, ongoing visceral input lowers the threshold of spinal neurons so that normally subthreshold somatic input is felt as pain.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain arises from convergence and facilitation of visceral and somatic inputs centrally.
questions.modelAnswer: Convergence-projection theory: visceral and somatic afferents from the same spinal segment converge on the same second-order neuron in the dorsal horn, so the brain misinterprets visceral pain as coming from the corresponding somatic (skin) area. Convergence-facilitation theory: continuous visceral afferent input facilitates (sensitises) spinal neurons, making them hyperexcitable, so that even weak somatic input is perceived as pain in the skin area.

questions.text: Describe the functions and the effect of a lesion of Somatosensory Area 2 (S2). (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: The secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) receives input from both sides of the body and works with S1 in interpreting sensation. It contributes to the perception of pain, temperature and crude touch and to integrative tasks such as tactile recognition. Because of its bilateral representation, a lesion impairs recognising and localising stimuli on both sides rather than just the contralateral side.
questions.keyConcept: S2 mediates bilateral crude sensation and higher-order processing, so lesions impair bilateral recognition.
questions.modelAnswer: Functions: responsible for the perception of pain, temperature and crude touch, and is involved in higher-order sensory processing. Lesion effect: impairment in recognising or localising stimuli on both sides of the body (bilateral effects).

questions.text: Describe the central analgesia system, its components and their neurotransmitters.
questions.explanation: The central analgesia (descending pain-modulating) system suppresses pain by sequential activation of the PVA, PAG, RMN and dorsal-horn PIC. Their neurotransmitters (beta-endorphins, enkephalin and serotonin) ultimately inhibit transmission from the type C and A-delta pain afferents at the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: The central analgesia system inhibits pain via PVA, PAG, RMN and dorsal-horn PIC.
questions.modelAnswer: Components: the periventricular area (PVA) of the hypothalamus secreting beta-endorphins; the periaqueductal gray area (PAG) of the midbrain and pons secreting enkephalin; the raphe magnus nucleus (RMN) of the pons and medulla secreting serotonin; and the pain inhibitory complex (PIC) in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord secreting enkephalin, which produces presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition of the incoming type C and A-delta pain fibers.

questions.text: Define headache and enumerate its intracranial causes.
questions.explanation: Headache represents referred pain originating from deep, pain-sensitive head structures. Its major intracranial causes include meningeal irritation and space-occupying lesions, altered CSF pressure, and vascular factors such as hypertension and migraine.
questions.keyConcept: Headache is referred pain from deep head structures with several intracranial causes.
questions.modelAnswer: Headache is pain referred to the surface of the head from deep head structures. Intracranial causes include: (1) meningitis, brain tumour and alcohol (toxic); (2) decreased CSF pressure; and (3) fever, hypertension and migraine.

questions.text: Which type of sensory receptors in the skin respond quickly at the onset of a stimulus but stop firing if the stimulus is constant?
questions.explanation: Rapidly adapting touch receptors fire briskly at stimulus onset and offset but cease during a steady stimulus. They detect movement and changing touch rather than constant pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting touch receptors respond mainly to changing stimuli.

questions.text: Which sensory receptor adapts rapidly to sustained skin stimulation?
questions.explanation: Touch receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles adapt rapidly to sustained skin stimulation. Pain and temperature receptors adapt slowly or not at all.
questions.keyConcept: Touch receptors adapt rapidly to sustained stimulation.

questions.text: Discrimination of stimulus intensity depends mainly on which of the following?
questions.explanation: Stronger stimuli recruit more receptors and afferent fibers, so intensity is coded mainly by the number of activated receptors. Higher firing frequency also contributes.
questions.keyConcept: Stimulus intensity is coded by the number of activated receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following explains areas with low two-point discrimination threshold?
questions.explanation: A low two-point discrimination threshold indicates high spatial acuity, which results from little convergence of afferent fibers onto each neuron. Each fiber serves a small receptive field.
questions.keyConcept: Low two-point threshold reflects little afferent convergence and small receptive fields.
options: Less convergence of afferent nerve fibers
More convergence of afferent nerve fibers

questions.text: Which of the following stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Local increase of potassium released from damaged cells depolarizes and stimulates nociceptors. Potassium is a key chemical mediator of pain.
questions.keyConcept: Increased extracellular potassium stimulates pain receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding sensory fiber conduction is correct?
questions.explanation: Crude (non-discriminative) touch is carried by thinly myelinated A-delta fibers in the spinothalamic system. Fine touch and vibration travel on large A-beta fibers in the dorsal columns.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch travels on A-delta fibers.
options: Crude touch is carried on Aδfibers
Fine touch is carried on C fibers
Fine touch is carried on Aδfibers
Vibration sense is carried on Aδfibers
Nociceptive stimuli are carried on Aβ fibers

questions.text: Which type of pain is transmitted by Aδnerve fibers?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers conduct fast, sharp, well-localized first pain. Slow burning pain is carried by unmyelinated C fibers.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers transmit fast, sharp pain.

questions.text: Sudden increase in skin temperature above 50 degrees Celsius leads to ……
questions.explanation: Skin temperatures above about 45–50°C activate thermal nociceptors and are perceived as pain. This protects tissue from thermal injury.
questions.keyConcept: Temperatures above ~45°C stimulate thermal nociceptors.
options: Transient impulses due to damage of cold receptors above 40 degrees Celsius

questions.text: Which fibers transmit crude touch sensation?
questions.explanation: Crude touch sensation is transmitted by A-delta fibers via the spinothalamic pathway. Discriminative touch instead uses large A-beta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers transmit crude touch sensation.

questions.text: Which substance stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Kinins, particularly bradykinin, are potent chemical activators of nociceptors released during tissue injury. They directly excite pain endings.
questions.keyConcept: Kinins such as bradykinin stimulate pain receptors.

questions.text: Which nerve fibers transmit warm temperature sensation?
questions.explanation: Warm temperature sensation is carried by unmyelinated C fibers. Cold sensation uses faster A-delta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: C fibers transmit warm temperature sensation.

questions.text: Fast pain is characterized by which duration?
questions.explanation: Fast pain is sharp and brief, lasting only a short time after the stimulus. It is conducted rapidly by A-delta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is sharp and short-lasting.

questions.text: Which of the following sensory modalities is primarily perceived at the level of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: Crude, poorly localized sensation can be appreciated at the level of the thalamus. Fine discriminative modalities require the cerebral cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Crude sensation is perceived at the thalamic level.

questions.text: Which clinical sign is seen in chronic gastritis due to inflammation of the stomach wall?
questions.explanation: Inflammation of the stomach wall in chronic gastritis produces reflex rigidity of the overlying abdominal muscles (visceral guarding). This protective spasm reflects visceral-somatic reflex activity.
questions.keyConcept: Gastric inflammation causes reflex rigidity of overlying muscles.

questions.text: In secondary hyperalgesia, which of the following describes the affected area?
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperalgesia is increased pain sensitivity in the normal skin surrounding the injured area. It arises from central sensitization rather than local tissue damage.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary hyperalgesia affects normal skin around the injury.
options: Inflamed tissue directly exposed to noxious stimuli
All dermatomes sharing the same dorsal root ganglion

questions.text: Which of the following explains pain relief when you rub the skin near an injury?
questions.explanation: Rubbing near an injury activates large A-beta fibers that inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn. This is explained by the gate control theory of pain.
questions.keyConcept: Rubbing relieves pain through gate control inhibition.

questions.text: A woman was wearing a dress on the beach. Later, when she wore a jacket over the same area, she felt pain. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: After sunburn, tissue products lower the nociceptor threshold so that a normally innocuous stimulus like clothing becomes painful. This is primary hyperalgesia from increased receptor sensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Tissue products increase nociceptor sensitivity, causing primary hyperalgesia.
options: Increase receptor sensitivity by tissue products
Activity-dependent increase in excitability of dorsal horn neurons
Increased threshold of peripheral nociceptors due to inflammatory mediators
Decreased inhibitory interneuron function in the spinal cord
Impaired saltatory conduction in primary afferent neurons

questions.text: Which receptors inhibit pain sensation in the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: Opioid receptors in the central nervous system bind endogenous and exogenous opioids to inhibit pain transmission. They are concentrated in the pain-modulating pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid receptors inhibit central pain transmission.

questions.text: Extracranial headache is an example of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Extracranial headache is felt at a site distant from the actual source, making it a form of referred pain. Pain from extracranial structures is projected to the head surface.
questions.keyConcept: Extracranial headache is a form of referred pain.

questions.text: The pain analgesic system includes which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Periaqueductal gray neurons of the analgesic system release enkephalin to inhibit pain pathways. Enkephalin activates downstream serotonergic projections.
questions.keyConcept: Periaqueductal gray neurons secrete enkephalin in the analgesic system.
options: Local cord neurons which secret serotonin
Local cord neurons which secrete endorphin

questions.text: Acupuncture relieves pain mainly by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Acupuncture relieves pain by activating the gate control mechanism and a psychogenic (expectation) component. Stimulation of large fibers closes the spinal pain gate.
questions.keyConcept: Acupuncture works through gate control and psychogenic mechanisms.
options: Gate control theory and psychogenic excitation
Blockade of sodium channels in sensory nerves

questions.text: Deep pain is typically characterized by which of the following features?
questions.explanation: Deep pain from muscles, joints and viscera is diffuse and poorly localized. It is often accompanied by autonomic responses.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pain is poorly localized.
options: Rapidly conducted by A delta fibers only

questions.text: Which of the following is correctly matched regarding the pain analgesic system?
questions.explanation: The nucleus raphe magnus uses serotonin to drive descending pain inhibition. Its serotonergic fibers project to the dorsal horn.
questions.keyConcept: The nucleus raphe magnus uses serotonin for pain inhibition.
options: Nucleus reticularis paragigantocellularis→ Gamma aminobutyric acid

questions.text: Referred pain from the gallbladder is most commonly felt in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: Gallbladder pain is referred to the right shoulder and inferior scapular region via the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). This reflects shared dermatomal innervation of the diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: Gallbladder pain refers to the right shoulder.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of extracranial headache?
questions.explanation: Otitis media is an extracranial source of headache because the pain arises outside the cranial cavity. Meningeal irritation and subarachnoid hemorrhage cause intracranial headache.
questions.keyConcept: Otitis media is a cause of extracranial headache.

questions.text: The initial phase of a migraine attack is associated with which of the following vascular events?
questions.explanation: The initial (aura) phase of migraine is associated with cerebral vasoconstriction. The subsequent throbbing headache phase involves vasodilation.
questions.keyConcept: Migraine begins with cerebral vasoconstriction.

questions.text: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
questions.explanation: Stereognosis, the recognition of objects by touch, depends on discriminative input from the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway. It requires fine touch and proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Stereognosis is carried by the dorsal column pathway.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding deep pressure sensation?
questions.explanation: Deep pressure sensation is mediated by slowly adapting receptors that maintain firing during sustained stimuli. This allows continuous monitoring of pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pressure is sensed by slowly adapting receptors.
options: It is mediated by slowly adapting receptors
It is transmitted only by free nerve endings
It adapts rapidly to sustained stimulus
It is carried exclusively by A delta fibers
It is not associated with vibration

questions.text: Which of the following does not contain channels that are activated by mechanical distortion:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (e) Cones. This is the option that does not fit the stem (the exception/incorrect statement), while the remaining choices are all true in this context.
questions.keyConcept: Which of the following does not contain channels that are activated by mechanical distortion

questions.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (c) Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold. Among the listed options this is the choice that best matches the stem, and the other options are incorrect distractors.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors
options: Receptors are non-specific to stimuli according to Muller’s law.
Stimulation of certain receptors can produces different modalities of sensations
Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold.
Receptor potential is inversely related to the intensity of stimulus according to Weber- Fechner law.
The same receptor may be stimulated by different stimuli to produce different sensations.

questions.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (d) Slowly adapting receptors help in body protection. Among the listed options this is the choice that best matches the stem, and the other options are incorrect distractors.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors
options: The magnitude of receptor potential and the magnitude of action potentials discharged in afferent nerve are directly related to logarithm of stimulus intensity.
Receptors that decrease their receptor potential rapidly in response to constant stimulation are tonic receptors.
Phasic receptors continue to discharge impulses even with a constant stimulus.
Slowly adapting receptors help in body protection.
Teleceptors detect cutaneous changes in environment.

questions.text: Compared to the back of the body, tip of finger is characterized by having:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (c) Less convergence of afferents. Among the listed options this is the choice that best matches the stem, and the other options are incorrect distractors.
questions.keyConcept: Compared to the back of the body, tip of finger is characterized by having
options: Less size of cortical representation area.

questions.text: Locality of the stimulus is discriminated by:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (d) Projection Theory. Among the listed options this is the choice that best matches the stem, and the other options are incorrect distractors.
questions.keyConcept: Locality of the stimulus is discriminated by

questions.text: Regarding sensations, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (a) Cutaneous sensations include touch, pain & proprioception. This is the option that does not fit the stem (the exception/incorrect statement), while the remaining choices are all true in this context.
questions.keyConcept: Sensations, all of the following are true EXCEPT
options: Cutaneous sensations include touch, pain & proprioception.
Tactile sensations include touch, pressure & vibration.
Kinesthetic sensations inciude sense of position and movement.

questions.text: Which of the following receptor is specific for the rate of movement:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (d) Paccinian corpuscle. Among the listed options this is the choice that best matches the stem, and the other options are incorrect distractors.
questions.keyConcept: Which of the following receptor is specific for the rate of movement
options: Receptors in capsules and ligaments of joints.

questions.text: Mention the mechanism of action of opioids.
questions.explanation: Opioids relieve pain by mimicking endogenous opioid peptides at mu, kappa and delta receptors coupled to inhibitory G-proteins. Presynaptically they reduce calcium entry and transmitter release such as substance P, while postsynaptically they increase potassium efflux to hyperpolarise neurons. Together these actions dampen nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn and enhance descending inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Opioids activate inhibitory opioid receptors, reducing neurotransmitter release and hyperpolarising neurons to block pain.
questions.modelAnswer: Opioids act as agonists at opioid receptors (mu, kappa and delta), which are G-protein-coupled receptors. Activation closes voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic nerve terminals (reducing neurotransmitter release) and opens potassium channels postsynaptically (causing hyperpolarisation). The net effect is decreased neuronal excitability and inhibition of pain transmission, including activation of the descending analgesic pathways.

questions.text: Mention two of the stimulatory pharmacological actions of morphine.
questions.explanation: Although morphine is mainly a CNS depressant, it has several stimulatory (excitatory) actions on specific centres. It stimulates the Edinger-Westphal nucleus to produce the characteristic pinpoint pupils (miosis) and activates the chemoreceptor trigger zone to cause nausea and vomiting. It also raises the tone of gastrointestinal smooth muscle, contributing to constipation.
questions.keyConcept: Morphine's stimulatory actions include miosis and activation of the vomiting (chemoreceptor) trigger zone.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Miosis (pupillary constriction) due to stimulation of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus of the oculomotor nerve. 2) Stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone causing nausea and vomiting. (Other stimulatory actions include increased gastrointestinal smooth muscle tone leading to constipation and increased ADH release.)

questions.text: HISTO: One of the following is a character of the Merkel's tactile discs:
questions.explanation: Merkel cells are connected to the surrounding epidermal cells by desmosomes and act as slowly adapting touch receptors. They are unencapsulated cutaneous receptors, not proprioceptors.
questions.keyConcept: Merkel cells attach to epidermal cells by desmosomes.
options: The nerve fiber penetrates between the epidermal cells
They are found between the prickle cell layer of the epidermis

questions.text: A lesion affecting Lamina IX of the spinal cord would primarily disrupt:
questions.explanation: Rexed lamina IX contains the alpha and gamma motor neurons of the anterior horn that supply skeletal muscle. A lesion here disrupts somatic motor output.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina IX houses motor neurons for somatic motor output.

questions.text: In the spinal cord, which of the following laminae corresponds to the main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius)?
questions.explanation: The nucleus proprius, the main sensory nucleus of the dorsal horn, lies mainly in Rexed lamina III (and IV). Lamina II corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa.
questions.keyConcept: The nucleus proprius corresponds to lamina III.

questions.text: The anterior horn cells are classified as:
questions.explanation: Anterior horn cells are large multipolar somatic efferent (motor) neurons whose axons leave in the ventral root to supply skeletal muscle. They are not sensory or visceral neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn cells are somatic efferent motor neurons.

questions.text: The dorsal nucleus of Clarke is most prominent at which spinal cord levels?
questions.explanation: Clarke's column is best developed between segments C8 and L3, where it gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. It is absent above C8 and below L3.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus is most prominent at C8-L3.

questions.text: The phrenic nucleus, which innervates the diaphragm, is part of which nuclear group?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nucleus is a member of the central group of anterior horn nuclei in cervical segments C3-C5. Its axons form the phrenic nerve supplying the diaphragm.
questions.keyConcept: The phrenic nucleus belongs to the central nuclear group.

questions.text: Which group of anterior horn nuclei innervates axial (trunk) muscles?
questions.explanation: The medial group of anterior horn cells supplies the axial muscles of the neck and trunk. The lateral groups instead supply the limb musculature.
questions.keyConcept: The medial anterior horn group innervates axial muscles.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei is located in the intermediate gray matter and acts as a relay for visceral afferent impulses?
questions.explanation: The intermedio-medial nucleus lies in the intermediate gray matter and relays visceral afferent information. The intermedio-lateral nucleus, in contrast, gives rise to preganglionic autonomic fibers.
questions.keyConcept: The intermedio-medial nucleus relays visceral afferents.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei is located in the posterior horn and involved in pain modulation?
questions.explanation: The substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) caps the posterior horn and is a key site for modulation of pain transmission. It is central to the gate control mechanism of pain.
questions.keyConcept: The substantia gelatinosa modulates pain in the posterior horn.

questions.text: Which spinal cord segment contains the lateral horn of gray matter?
questions.explanation: The lateral horn is present in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments (T1-L2/3), housing preganglionic sympathetic neurons. A smaller sacral autonomic column exists at S2-S4 but is not a true lateral horn.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral horn is found in thoracic and upper lumbar segments.

questions.text: Which type of spinal cord neuron has long axons that leave the gray matter to form tracts?
questions.explanation: Golgi type I neurons have long axons that leave the gray matter to form ascending or descending tracts. Golgi type II neurons are short-axoned interneurons confined to the gray matter.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi type I neurons have long axons that form tracts.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei is located in lamina VII of the gray matter of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus lies in lamina VII and gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. The posteromarginal nucleus, substantia gelatinosa and main sensory nucleus occupy laminae I, II and III-IV respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus is located in lamina VII.

questions.text: Which of the following best characterizes the Ruffini corpuscle?
questions.explanation: The Ruffini corpuscle is a thinly encapsulated, slowly adapting receptor in which nerve fibers branch among a core of collagen fibers. Concentric lamellae instead characterize the Pacinian corpuscle.
questions.keyConcept: Ruffini corpuscle nerve fibers end among a core of collagen fibers.
options: The nerve fiber ends in between a core of collagen fibers
It is present in the dermal papillae
It is a non-capsulated nerve ending

questions.text: Compare between Pacinian and Meissner's corpuscles.
questions.explanation: Both are encapsulated cutaneous mechanoreceptors but differ in location and structure. Meissner's corpuscles lie superficially in the dermal papillae and detect fine discriminative touch, with transversely stacked Schwann cells. Pacinian corpuscles lie deep in the dermis and detect pressure and vibration, recognisable by their thick onion-like concentric lamellae.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's (superficial) senses fine touch; Pacinian (deep, lamellated) senses pressure and vibration.
questions.modelAnswer: Meissner's corpuscle - Site: dermal papillae of skin; Nerve: loses its myelin outside the capsule, runs spirally, and ends in an expanded knob; Teloglia: transversely arranged flattened modified Schwann cells. Pacinian corpuscle - Site: deep dermis; Nerve: loses its myelin inside the capsule, runs axially to the opposite pole, with a club-like termination; Teloglia: concentric layers of flattened modified Schwann cells (two cores).

questions.text: Enumerate the non-capsulated (unencapsulated) receptors and describe one of them.
questions.explanation: Unencapsulated receptors lack a connective-tissue capsule around the nerve ending. They include free nerve endings for pain, temperature and crude touch, peritrichial endings around hair follicles, and Merkel discs for fine touch. Free nerve endings are the simplest and most widespread, formed by bare axons that ramify among epithelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Unencapsulated receptors are free nerve endings, peritrichial endings, and Merkel discs.
questions.modelAnswer: Unencapsulated receptors: 1) free nerve endings; 2) peritrichial (hair follicle) nerve endings; 3) Merkel's tactile discs. Free nerve endings: the afferent nerve fibres arise from the subepidermal nerve plexus and lose their myelin and neurilemmal sheaths; the naked fibres penetrate the epidermis and run between epidermal cells, terminating as small knobs (reaching the superficial layers in the cornea).

questions.text: Classify the different types of cutaneous receptors, with examples.
questions.explanation: Cutaneous receptors are grouped by whether a capsule surrounds the nerve terminal. Unencapsulated types (free nerve endings, Merkel discs, peritrichial endings) generally mediate pain, temperature and simple touch. Encapsulated types (Meissner, Pacinian, Ruffini, Krause) are specialised for touch, pressure, vibration and stretch.
questions.keyConcept: Cutaneous receptors are unencapsulated (free, Merkel, peritrichial) or encapsulated (Meissner, Pacinian, Ruffini, Krause).
questions.modelAnswer: Cutaneous receptors are classified into: Unencapsulated receptors - free nerve endings, Merkel's tactile discs, and peritrichial nerve endings. Encapsulated receptors - Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles, Ruffini corpuscles, and Krause end bulbs.

questions.text: Describe the histological structure and function of Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles.
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are superficial, rapidly adapting receptors whose stacked Schwann cells suit them to fine two-point discrimination. Pacinian corpuscles are deep, large, onion-like receptors whose lamellated capsule makes them respond to pressure and high-frequency vibration. Both are encapsulated mechanoreceptors that adapt quickly to stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's senses fine touch superficially; Pacinian senses pressure and vibration in the deep dermis.
questions.modelAnswer: Meissner's corpuscle: located in the dermal papillae, ovoid, with transversely stacked modified Schwann cells; mediates touch and tactile discrimination. Pacinian corpuscle: located in the deep dermis, large, with concentric lamellae forming an inner core and an outer core of Schwann cells; detects pressure and vibration.

questions.text: Describe the organization of the motor nuclei in the anterior horn and their muscle targets.
questions.explanation: The somatic motor neurons of the anterior (ventral) horn are organised somatotopically into medial, central and lateral cell columns. The medial group innervates axial musculature and the lateral group innervates the limbs, while the central group contains specialised nuclei such as the phrenic and accessory nuclei. This arrangement matches proximal-to-distal motor control along the cord.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn motor nuclei are medial (axial), central (phrenic/accessory), and lateral (limb) groups.
questions.modelAnswer: The anterior horn motor neurons are arranged in groups: Medial group - supplies axial (trunk) muscles. Central group - includes the phrenic nucleus (diaphragm) and the spinal accessory nucleus. Lateral group - supplies the limb muscles.

questions.text: Describe the motor nuclei of the anterior horn (types and groups).
questions.explanation: Anterior horn cells comprise large alpha motor neurons that drive extrafusal muscle fibres and smaller gamma motor neurons that set muscle spindle sensitivity. These neurons are clustered into medial, central and lateral nuclear groups. The medial group serves axial muscles while the lateral group expands at the limb enlargements to serve the extremities.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn contains alpha and gamma neurons in medial, central, and lateral nuclear groups.
questions.modelAnswer: Types: alpha neurons (supply extrafusal muscle fibres) and gamma neurons (supply intrafusal fibres of the muscle spindle). Groups: Medial group (anteromedial and posteromedial nuclei), Central group (central and anterior nuclei), and Lateral group (anterolateral, posterolateral and retroposterolateral nuclei).

questions.text: Discuss the lateral horn and its functional significance.
questions.explanation: The lateral horn is a small lateral projection of gray matter found only in the thoracolumbar cord (T1-L3). Its intermediolateral nucleus houses preganglionic sympathetic neurons whose axons leave via the ventral roots and white rami. This makes the lateral horn the spinal origin of the sympathetic nervous system.
questions.keyConcept: The lateral horn (T1-L3) contains the intermediolateral nucleus giving preganglionic sympathetic fibres.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral horn is present in spinal segments T1-L3. It contains the intermediolateral nucleus, which gives rise to the preganglionic sympathetic (visceral efferent) fibres. It is therefore the source of sympathetic outflow from the spinal cord.

questions.text: Enumerate the nuclei of the posterior horn.
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) horn processes incoming sensory information and contains several named nuclei arranged dorsoventrally. The posteromarginal nucleus and substantia gelatinosa handle pain and temperature, the nucleus proprius relays touch and pressure, and Clarke's nucleus relays unconscious proprioception. The reticular and intermediomedial nuclei contribute to sensory integration.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior horn nuclei: posteromarginal, substantia gelatinosa, proprius, reticular, Clarke's, and intermediomedial.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Posteromarginal nucleus. 2) Substantia gelatinosa. 3) Nucleus proprius. 4) Reticular nucleus. 5) Clarke's nucleus (nucleus dorsalis). 6) Intermediomedial nucleus.

questions.text: Differentiate between Golgi type I and Golgi type II neurons in the spinal cord gray matter.
questions.explanation: Neurons are classified by axon length into Golgi type I and type II. Type I cells, such as anterior horn motor neurons and projection (tract) cells, send long axons over considerable distances. Type II cells are small interneurons with short axons confined to the local gray matter, where they integrate and modulate signals.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi type I neurons have long projecting axons; type II are short-axon local interneurons.
questions.modelAnswer: Golgi type I neurons: have long axons that leave the gray matter to form tracts (e.g., motor neurons and tract cells). Golgi type II neurons: have short axons that remain locally, acting as interneurons.

questions.text: Mention four major nuclei of the spinal cord gray matter and identify their corresponding laminae.
questions.explanation: Rexed divided the spinal gray matter into ten laminae, several of which correspond to classic named nuclei. The posteromarginal nucleus and substantia gelatinosa occupy laminae I and II, the nucleus proprius lies in laminae III-IV, and lamina VII contains Clarke's and intermediolateral nuclei. The motor neuron groups of the anterior horn form lamina IX.
questions.keyConcept: Named spinal nuclei map onto Rexed laminae I, II, III-IV, VII, and IX.
questions.modelAnswer: Lamina I: posteromarginal nucleus. Lamina II: substantia gelatinosa. Laminae III-IV: nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus). Lamina VII: Clarke's nucleus and the intermediolateral nucleus. Lamina IX: anterior horn motor cell groups.

questions.text: Describe the microscopic structure of the muscle spindle. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The muscle spindle is an encapsulated proprioceptive stretch receptor embedded among ordinary muscle fibres. Its fusiform connective-tissue capsule encloses a small number of specialised intrafusal fibres of the nuclear bag and nuclear chain types. Because the spindle lies parallel to the extrafusal fibres, it is stretched whenever the muscle lengthens, allowing it to signal changes in muscle length.
questions.keyConcept: The muscle spindle is an encapsulated fusiform receptor containing parallel intrafusal fibres.
questions.modelAnswer: Shape: fusiform (spindle-shaped). Capsule: enclosed by a connective tissue capsule (encapsulated). Contents: contains 2-12 specialised intrafusal muscle fibres (nuclear bag and nuclear chain types). Orientation: the intrafusal fibres lie parallel to the surrounding extrafusal muscle fibres.

questions.text: Describe the histological structure of the Pacinian corpuscle. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The Pacinian corpuscle is a large, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor that detects deep pressure and vibration. Histologically it has an onion-like appearance, with concentric lamellae of flattened cells and fluid surrounding a single central unmyelinated nerve terminal. The lamellar capsule filters out steady pressure, making the receptor respond mainly to changing (vibratory) stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: The Pacinian corpuscle is an onion-like lamellated mechanoreceptor with a central nerve ending.
questions.modelAnswer: Type: an encapsulated, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor (a lamellated corpuscle). Capsule: a thick connective tissue capsule. Lamellae: multiple concentric lamellae arranged like an onion, formed by flattened cells and collagen separated by fluid. Core: a single central non-myelinated nerve ending.

questions.text: Name two receptors found in the epidermis. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: The epidermis contains sensory structures despite being avascular and largely cellular. Merkel cells, associated with nerve terminals as Merkel discs, are slowly adapting receptors for fine touch and texture. Free nerve endings extend into the epidermis and detect pain, temperature and crude touch.
questions.keyConcept: Epidermal receptors include Merkel cells (discs) and free nerve endings.
questions.modelAnswer: Merkel cells (Merkel discs). Free nerve endings.

questions.text: Enumerate the encapsulated and unencapsulated receptors. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Cutaneous and deep receptors are classified by whether a connective-tissue capsule surrounds the nerve ending. Encapsulated receptors such as Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles and muscle spindles have specialised capsules that tune their responses. Unencapsulated (free) endings, including bare nerve endings and Merkel discs, lack such capsules and mediate pain, temperature and simple touch.
questions.keyConcept: Encapsulated receptors have capsules (Pacinian, Meissner, spindle) while unencapsulated ones do not.
questions.modelAnswer: Encapsulated receptors: Pacinian corpuscle, Meissner's corpuscle, and the muscle spindle. Unencapsulated receptors: free nerve endings and Merkel discs.

questions.text: List the nuclei forming lamina VII of the spinal gray matter. (2 Marks)
questions.explanation: Lamina VII is a large zone of the intermediate spinal gray matter described by Rexed. It houses several functionally distinct nuclei: Clarke's column for unconscious proprioception, the intermediolateral nucleus for sympathetic outflow, the intermediomedial nucleus for visceral afferent integration, and the sacral autonomic nuclei for parasympathetic outflow. Their segmental levels reflect the distribution of autonomic and proprioceptive functions.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lamina VII contains Clarke's column and the intermediolateral, intermediomedial and sacral autonomic nuclei.
questions.modelAnswer: Clarke's column (nucleus dorsalis): C8-L3; relays unconscious proprioception. Intermediolateral nucleus: T1-L3; contains sympathetic preganglionic neurons. Intermediomedial nucleus: receives visceral afferents. Sacral autonomic nuclei: S2-S4; contain parasympathetic preganglionic neurons.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes a feature of Pacinian corpuscles compared to Meissner corpuscles?
questions.explanation: In Pacinian corpuscles the afferent fiber runs axially through the lamellated capsule, whereas in Meissner corpuscles the fiber follows a coiled, tortuous course. This structural difference suits their different functions.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian fibers run axially while Meissner fibers are coiled.

questions.text: Which receptors provide the sense of movement and position of the body?
questions.explanation: Proprioceptive receptors such as muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs sense body movement and position. They provide feedback for posture and coordination.

questions.text: Which type of mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting vibration?

questions.text: Describe shape of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Shape of spinal cord.
questions.modelAnswer:
Shape of the spinal cord: It is a roughly cylindrical, slightly flattened (anteroposteriorly) structure occupying the upper two-thirds of the vertebral canal. It extends from the foramen magnum (continuous with the medulla oblongata) to the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) in adults, where it tapers as the conus medullaris. It shows two fusiform enlargements: the cervical enlargement (C3–T2) for the brachial plexus/upper limb, and the lumbosacral enlargement (L1–S3) for the lumbosacral plexus/lower limb. From the conus the filum terminale descends to the coccyx.

questions.modelAnswer:
Site of exit of spinal nerves from the vertebral column: The 31 pairs of spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina. questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lumbar puncture: A needle is introduced into the subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid. Because the spinal cord ends at L1 in adults, the puncture is performed below this level (between the L3–L4 or L4–L5 spines, at the level of the supracristal/Tuffier's line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, which crosses the L4 spine) to avoid injuring the cord; here only the cauda equina floats in the lumbar cistern. questions.text: Describe lamination of pyramidal tract in cerebral cortex, internal capsule, brain stem & spinal cord.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Lamination of pyramidal tract in cerebral cortex, internal capsule, brain stem & spinal cord.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lamination of the pyramidal (corticospinal) tract: In the cerebral cortex it arises mainly from the precentral gyrus (area 4) and adjacent areas, somatotopically arranged (lower limb in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface, then trunk, upper limb and face laterally – the motor homunculus). In the internal capsule the fibres are compactly arranged in the genu (corticonuclear) and the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb (corticospinal), with the upper limb fibres anterior and the lower limb fibres posterior. In the brain stem (crus cerebri/midbrain) they occupy the middle two-thirds of the crus; in the pons they are broken into bundles by the pontine nuclei; in the medulla they form the pyramid. In the spinal cord, after the pyramidal decussation, the lateral corticospinal tract lies in the lateral white column, laminated with cervical (upper limb) fibres medial and sacral fibres lateral.

questions.text: Describe termination of pyramidal tract.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Termination of pyramidal tract.
questions.modelAnswer:
Termination of the pyramidal tract: The corticospinal fibres descend through the internal capsule, crus cerebri, pons and medulla. At the lower medulla about 80–90% of fibres cross in the pyramidal (motor) decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract, which descends in the lateral white column and ends by synapsing (directly or through interneurons) on the anterior horn motor cells throughout the cord, supplying chiefly the limb muscles. The uncrossed 10–20% form the anterior corticospinal tract, which descends in the anterior white column and crosses segmentally in the anterior white commissure before ending on anterior horn cells supplying axial/trunk muscles. The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibres end on the motor cranial nerve nuclei in the brain stem.

questions.modelAnswer:
Corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract: It arises from the lower part of the precentral gyrus (head region of the motor cortex), descends through the genu of the internal capsule and the crus cerebri, and ends on the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves (CN III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII) in the brain stem, mostly bilaterally. Clinically important exception: the part of the facial nucleus supplying the muscles of the lower half of the face receives only crossed (contralateral) fibres, while the upper-face part is bilaterally supplied; hence an upper motor neuron lesion spares the upper face but paralyses the contralateral lower face.

Differences between upper and lower motor neuron lesions: In an UPPER motor neuron lesion there is spastic paralysis, increased (exaggerated) deep tendon reflexes, a positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar), loss of superficial reflexes, marked hypertonia (clasp-knife), no/minimal muscle wasting (only disuse atrophy) and no fasciculations. questions.text: Describe the effect of complete transection of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: The effect of complete transection of spinal cord.
questions.modelAnswer:
Effect of complete transection of the spinal cord: There is total loss of all sensations and voluntary movement below the level of the lesion. Initially there is a stage of spinal shock (flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and retention of urine) lasting days to weeks, followed by recovery of reflex activity with spastic paraplegia (or quadriplegia if cervical), exaggerated tendon reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses. There is loss of voluntary bladder and bowel control (automatic reflex bladder develops) and loss of all sensation below the lesion.

questions.modelAnswer:
Clinical picture of Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal hemisection): Below the level of the lesion – on the SAME (ipsilateral) side: spastic paralysis (UMN signs) due to corticospinal tract damage, and loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception due to posterior column damage. On the OPPOSITE (contralateral) side: loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning one or two segments below the lesion (lateral spinothalamic tract). questions.modelAnswer:
Afferents and efferents of the corpus striatum: The neostriatum (caudate nucleus + putamen) is the main receptive part – it receives afferents from the whole cerebral cortex (corticostriate fibres), from the thalamus (centromedian nucleus) and from the substantia nigra (nigrostriatal dopaminergic fibres). The globus pallidus (paleostriatum) is the main effector/outflow part – it sends efferents to the thalamus (ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei), to the subthalamic nucleus and to the substantia nigra; from the thalamus the influence is relayed to the motor cortex.

questions.text: Describe substantia nigra.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia nigra.
questions.modelAnswer:
Substantia nigra: It is a large motor nucleus in the midbrain lying between the crus cerebri (ventrally) and the tegmentum (dorsally), extending through the whole length of the midbrain. It has two parts: a darkly pigmented (melanin-containing) pars compacta dorsally and a pars reticulata ventrally. It is connected reciprocally with the corpus striatum (the nigrostriatal pathway is dopaminergic). Degeneration of its dopaminergic neurons causes Parkinson's disease.

questions.text: Mention function & blood supply of corpus striatum.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Function & blood supply of corpus striatum.
questions.modelAnswer:
Function and blood supply of the corpus striatum: Function – it is part of the extrapyramidal system; it controls and regulates voluntary movement, muscle tone and posture, and suppresses unwanted movements; lesions cause dyskinesias (e.g. chorea, athetosis, Parkinsonian rigidity). Blood supply – mainly from the central (striate) branches of the middle cerebral artery (the lateral striate / lenticulostriate arteries) and from the medial striate artery (recurrent artery of Heubner) of the anterior cerebral artery, with contributions from the anterior choroidal artery.

(AI model answer), Answers are not in the anatomy department book

questions.text: Describe connections & function of the different functional lobes of the cerebellum.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Connections & function of the different functional lobes of the cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer:
Connections and functions of the functional lobes of the cerebellum: (1) Archicerebellum (flocculonodular lobe / vestibulocerebellum) – connected with the vestibular nerve and nuclei; controls equilibrium and balance and eye movements; its lesion causes truncal ataxia and nystagmus. (2) Paleocerebellum (anterior lobe + parts of vermis / spinocerebellum) – receives spinocerebellar input; controls muscle tone and posture; its lesion disturbs tone and gait. (3) Neocerebellum (posterior/middle lobe / cerebrocerebellum) – connected with the cerebral cortex through the pontine nuclei; coordinates fine, skilled voluntary movement; its lesion causes the signs of neocerebellar deficit (dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, hypotonia) on the same side.

(AI model answer), Answers are not in the anatomy department book

questions.text: Describe blood supply of cerebellum.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Blood supply of cerebellum.
questions.modelAnswer:
Blood supply of the cerebellum: by three pairs of arteries: (1) the superior cerebellar artery (from the basilar artery), (2) the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA, from the basilar artery), and (3) the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA, from the vertebral artery). They supply the cerebellar cortex, white matter and deep nuclei.

questions.text: Enumerate contents of superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Contents of superior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Contents of the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum): It is mainly an efferent (outflow) peduncle. It contains the efferent fibres from the dentate (and other deep) nuclei to the red nucleus and thalamus (dentatorubrothalamic tract), and the afferent anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract.

questions.text: Enumerate contents of middle cerebellar peduncle.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Contents of middle cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Contents of the middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis): It is entirely afferent. It carries the crossed pontocerebellar fibres – axons of the pontine nuclei that relay corticopontine information from the opposite cerebral cortex to the cerebellar cortex.

questions.text: Enumerate contents of inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.explanation: This is a long-answer anatomy question from the CNS module; a complete response should cover the points outlined in the model answer. It is classified under the chapter 'Motor System & Spinal Cord'.
questions.keyConcept: Contents of inferior cerebellar peduncle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Contents of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body): It is mainly afferent and carries: the posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract, the cuneocerebellar tract, the olivocerebellar fibres (from the inferior olivary nucleus), the vestibulocerebellar fibres, and reticulocerebellar fibres; its efferent component (juxtarestiform body) carries cerebellar fibres to the vestibular nuclei (cerebellovestibular and fastigiobulbar fibres).
